newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Crashed Dutch Dakota, a workhorse of the sky.
newsitem.headline: Crashed Dutch Dakota, a workhorse of the sky.

text.p: A lovingly restored DC-3 Dakota which crashed into the sea off the Dutch coast on Wednesday first took to the skies more than half a century ago.
Eleven thousand of the planes were built between 1935 and 1948 and around 1,000 of them are believed to be still flying with air forces, commercially or for fun.

The plane involved in Wednesday's crash was operated by a band of aviation enthusiasts known as the Dutch Dakota Association (DDA) which bought it in 1983 for 300,000 guilders ($160,000) and restored it to its former glory.
As well as air show displays, it was used for pleasure flights for DDA members and sponsors, regularly carrying up to 32 passengers and six crew.

Made by the Douglas Aircraft Corporation, Dakotas were traditionally equipped with two 1,200-horsepower Pratt and Whitney propeller engines which gave them a cruising speed of about 200 km per hour (125 mph).

The Dakota dominated the skies in the 1930s and 1940s, ferrying supplies during the Normandy landings in France in 1944 and the Berlin airlift of 1948. The ubiquitous plane was the mainstay of passenger fleets but it was far from luxurious.

Compared to modern aircraft it was noisy, slow, and unpressurised -- passengers had to wear breathing apparatus to fly over mountains. Journeys of any distance would take days rather than hours, although this was quicker than the sea journey of weeks.
The Dakota became the workhorse for cargo and passengers in every corner of the globe.

Its name, experts say, derives from a shortening of the plane's original title the Douglas Aircraft Corporation Transport Aircraft (DACoTA). This was soon corrupted to Dakota, after the U.S. state, by pilots of Britain's Royal Air Force.
The Dutch national airline KLM has fond memories of the earlier DC-2 version of the Dakota -- it won the historic London to Melbourne race in 1934 with one.
The usual Dakota interior has eight closely spaced bench seats on each side, next to square windows. They can be folded against the windows to allow room for cargo.
British entrepreneur Richard Branson, head of Virgin Atlantic Airways, has used them for pleasure flights in Florida.
In 1993 six Dakotas from Britain's Marine Pollution Control Unit were used to spray dispersant on an oil slick from a stricken tanker in the Shetland Islands.
